segments.narration: A million dollars is on offer to read five symbols. January 2025. Tamil Nadu's chief minister put up the prize.
The Indus script was written between roughly 2800 and 1900 BCE, across about four thousand seals, tablets and broken pots.
The problem is length. The average inscription runs five signs. Five. There is almost nothing to work with.
And there is no Rosetta Stone. Not one bilingual text has ever surfaced, and nobody knows what language these cities spoke.

More than a hundred decipherments have been published since the 1920s. The serious contenders split three ways: Dravidian, Indo-Aryan, or, per a 2004 paper, not writing at all. Until a longer text appears, five symbols is all anyone has.

verdicts.claim: In January 2025 Tamil Nadu Chief Minister M. K. Stalin announced a US$1 million prize for deciphering the Indus script.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia records the 2025 prize; Archaeology Magazine dates the announcement to January 2025 and names Stalin.

verdicts.claim: The Indus script dates to roughly 2800-1900 BCE and survives on about 4,000 inscribed seals, tablets and pottery fragments.

verdicts.claim: Indus inscriptions are very short, averaging around five signs.

verdicts.claim: No bilingual or digraphic Indus text has ever been found, and the underlying Harappan language has not been identified.
verdicts.note: 85% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article

verdicts.claim: More than 100 decipherment attempts have been published since the 1920s, with the main competing hypotheses being Dravidian, Indo-Aryan, and a 2004 argument by Farmer, Sproat and Witzel that the signs are not writing at all.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia gives more than 100 published attempts since the 1920s with no consensus, and names the Dravidian, Indo-Aryan and non-linguistic (Farmer, Sproat and Witzel 2004) hypotheses, the last disputed by Parpola and Rao et al. 2009.
